title: The prairie under the wheat
teaches: The Palouse prairie and what is left of it

blocks.text: Climb Steptoe Butte, north of Colfax in eastern Washington, and the Palouse lies around you in every direction: rounded hills like frozen waves, and on every one of them, to the horizon, wheat, barley, lentils and peas. In spring it is green, in summer gold, in autumn brown stubble. It is one of the most productive farmlands on Earth for crops grown without irrigation.

A hundred and fifty years ago it was all grassland. The **Palouse prairie** was a grassland of bunchgrasses, Idaho fescue and bluebunch wheatgrass, thick with wildflowers: arrowleaf balsamroot, lupines, shooting stars, and in the wetter hollows blue camas, whose bulbs the Nez Perce, Palouse and Spokane peoples dug and roasted[^camas]. Settlers began ploughing it in the 1870s. By the 1930s almost all of it had gone under the plough. Today far less than one percent is left.

The hills are made of **loess**, silt carried by the wind. During the ice ages, glaciers and the great Missoula floods spread fine rock flour across the Columbia Basin to the west; the prevailing winds picked it up and dropped it on the Palouse, tens of metres deep in places, over hundreds of thousands of years. The Geology course follows the floods; the Dirt course explains why silt makes such good soil. The prairie grasses, growing on it for thousands of years, added the dark, crumbly organic matter that made the soil rich. That is why the plough took it all: there was almost nowhere a farmer didn't want to farm.

The prairie that survives does so where ploughing was impossible or forbidden. It hangs on the steep upper slopes of buttes like Steptoe and Kamiak, which rise from the hills as islands of older rock[^steptoe]; on rocky knobs and in the corners of fields too awkward for machinery; along old railway lines; and in pioneer cemeteries, where the ground was never turned. Many remnants are a hectare or less. The largest are a few hundred hectares.

Lesson 19 showed what to expect of such patches. Each is an island in a sea of wheat. Lesson 18's species-area rule says how many kinds an island of its size can keep, and the extinction debt says it will take time to lose the rest. A small cemetery remnant has probably paid most of its debt already; a large butte top may still be losing species a century after the land around it was ploughed.

blocks.caption: Five sizes of prairie remnant, from a roadside strip to a preserve, against two species-area curves: what each held as part of the unbroken prairie, and what it can keep as an island in wheat. The remnants are illustrations, not measured sites. A model.
blocks.task: Move the years on from the ploughing

blocks.text: Remnants matter beyond their size. They hold seed of plants that could restore a field taken out of farming, and genes adapted to the Palouse's climate. Small reserves together can hold many kinds between them, as the single-large-or-several-small argument of lesson 19 found, especially of plants that need little room[^conservation].

In 1897 a naturalist described a large white earthworm from the Palouse, said to grow to a metre long. It was hardly ever seen again, and by the late twentieth century many assumed it was extinct, a casualty of the plough. Then in 2005 a graduate student at the University of Idaho dug one up, and in 2010 researchers found living adults in a prairie remnant. The worms they found were about 30 centimetres long, not a metre[^worm].

The worm is a reminder of how little is known about what lived in a lost ecosystem. The prairie's plants were collected and named; its soil animals, fungi and microbes mostly were not. Some may survive in the remnants, unknown; some will have gone without anyone noticing.

blocks.title: Outside
points: In May or June, visit Kamiak Butte County Park or Steptoe Butte State Park and walk the upper slopes. Look for balsamroot's big yellow flowers and the tight clumps of bunchgrass between them, then look down at the wheat fields below and imagine the whole view like the slope you are standing on.

blocks.caption: Five questions on the Palouse
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: How much of the Palouse prairie survives?
items.why: Almost all of it was ploughed between the 1870s and the 1930s.

items.ask: Why was nearly all the prairie ploughed?
choices: Its deep, rich loess soil was good for farming nearly everywhere
The grass was poisonous to cattle
items.why: Wind-blown silt and thousands of years of prairie grass made soil a farmer wanted everywhere.

choices: Steep butte tops, rocky knobs and old cemeteries
In the middle of the best fields
items.why: Places too steep, rocky or protected to plough.

items.ask: In the figure, why does a large remnant keep losing species for longer than a small one?
choices: Its larger populations die out more slowly, so its debt takes longer to pay
It was ploughed around more recently
items.why: Lesson 19: small patches pay their extinction debt fast, large ones slowly.

items.ask: What does the Palouse giant earthworm show?
choices: That soil animals of a lost prairie can survive unseen in its remnants
That the prairie is fully recovered
items.why: Thought extinct, it turned up in a remnant. Many soil animals were never recorded at all.

summary: **The Palouse was a bunchgrass prairie.** Fescue, wheatgrass, balsamroot and camas covered its hills.
**Far less than one percent survives.** Ploughing from the 1870s took almost all of it.
**Its hills are wind-blown silt, loess.** Rich and deep, there was almost nowhere a farmer didn't want to plough.
**Remnants hang on where ploughs couldn't go.** Butte tops, rocky knobs, field corners and cemeteries.
**Each remnant is an island paying an extinction debt.** Small ones have paid most of it; big ones are still paying.
**Much of what lived there was never recorded.** The giant earthworm, thought extinct, turned up in 2005.

conservation.title: Restoring the prairie
conservation.text: Some farmers and land trusts in the Palouse are sowing native seed, gathered from remnants, on land taken out of crops. A restored field is not the old prairie, but it can hold many of its plants and the insects that feed on them.

worm.title: The worm
worm.text: The Palouse giant earthworm, Driloleirus americanus, lives in deep burrows and is pale pink-white. Stories that it smells of lilies seem to have grown in the telling. How many survive, and where, is still unknown.

steptoe.title: A steptoe
steptoe.text: Steptoe Butte is a hill of old rock that the lava flows of the Columbia Plateau surrounded but never covered. Geologists borrowed its name for any such island of older rock poking up through younger lava: a steptoe.

camas.title: Camas
camas.text: Camas bulbs, slow-roasted in pits for a day or more, were a staple food for the peoples of the inland Northwest, and camas meadows were tended and harvested for generations. Lewis and Clark's party, starving after crossing the Bitterroot Mountains in 1805, was fed camas by the Nez Perce.
